title: How do you plan a product launch in a case interview?
description: "How should the client launch the product?" The client wants a plan to launch a product. If the question is whether to launch at all, use market entry.
hook: Product launch cases ask how to bring something new to market: who to sell it to, how, at what price and with what goal. Here is a structure that keeps all of that tidy.
body:
When you will use it

The client wants a plan to launch a product. If the question is whether to launch at all, use market entry.

This is a generate question: "How can we do this?" Lay out every option in buckets that don't overlap, size them, then pick the best few. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Who is it for, and what does the launch need to achieve?

The structure

  • Who to target
    • Segment size and growth
    • Competitors in the segment
    • Unmet needs
  • What to offer
    • Product
    • Price
    • Place (channels)
    • Promotion (message and brand)
  • How to roll it out
    • Capabilities (production · distribution · cash)
    • Pilot, then scale
  • Does it pay?
    • Expected sales
    • Costs and break-even

Make it your own

Pick the segment first: the 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion) all follow from who you are selling to.

The mistake to avoid

Choosing price and promotion before choosing the customer.

Practise with real prompts

1. How should a snack brand launch a high-protein bar?

Show a model structure
  • Who: Target customers and their need; Size of the segment
  • What: Product, flavours, pack sizes; Price vs rivals
  • Where and how: Channels: supermarkets, gyms, online; Marketing and sampling
  • Economics and risks: Volume to break even; Cannibalisation of our other bars

Where to start: Who: a launch without a clear target customer spreads money thin.

The trap: Starting with advertising before choosing the customer and the channel.

2. Should a supermarket launch a premium own-label range?

Show a model structure
  • Customer demand: Shoppers buying premium brands; Willingness to trust our brand
  • Economics: Margin vs branded products; Volume needed to cover development
  • Suppliers: Who can make it at quality; Reaction of big brands
  • Cannibalisation: Sales taken from our standard own-label; Net margin gained

Where to start: Margin vs branded: premium own-label usually earns more per item.

The trap: Ignoring how the big brands might react, such as cutting promotions.

3. Should a business school launch a fully online MBA?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Students who can't study on campus; Price they would pay
  • Competition: Other online MBAs and their prices; Our brand vs theirs
  • Economics: Development and teaching cost; Students needed to break even
  • Cannibalisation and brand: Cannibalising our campus MBA; Perceived quality and rankings

Where to start: Cannibalisation of the campus MBA, often the school's flagship programme.

The trap: Assuming online students are all new.
